summary:
SPHEREx Sky Navigator is a web application that makes NASA’s infrared observations accessible through interactive sky exploration and detailed image inspection.
Built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, React Three Fiber, and Zustand, the frontend renders a celestial panorama and calculates ICRS coordinates directly from the camera’s viewing direction. HiPS imagery, organized through HEALPix, streams from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), loading tiles according to position and zoom level. Users can explore SPHEREx spectral channels spanning approximately 0.75–5.0 μm and locate galaxies through NED.
 A Python/FastAPI backend queries SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 observations using persistent background jobs and SQLite metadata storage. For comparison, scientific FITS cutouts are processed with Astropy and resampled onto a common north-up, east-left grid. A chronological slideshow displays individual observations alongside timestamps and detector information.
Nearby-region searches, a weekly M101 challenge, separate metadata and image caches, bounded requests, and retry mechanisms supportexploration and recovery during archive interruptions.
Guided steps and plain-language explanations help beginners navigate real astronomical data. The current version supports visual inspection; calibrated change detection and image subtraction remain future objectives.
details:
SPHEREx Sky Navigator helps people explore NASA’s infrared observations without requiring specialist astronomy knowledge. Users navigate an interactive sky map, search for galaxies, change infrared wavelengths, and inspect observations of a selected region through a chronological slideshow.

The application uses HiPS tiles organized with HEALPix for efficient sky navigation. Detailed inspection uses FITS cutouts, processed with Astropy and aligned onto a common coordinate grid. Data comes from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive, while NED resolves galaxy names.

We developed the frontend using TypeScript, Next.js, React, React Three Fiber, Three.js, and Zustand. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, and SQLite, with Docker supporting deployment. Users need a modern browser with WebGL support; no telescope or dedicated astronomy software is required.

Our creative approach connects panoramic exploration, infrared wavelength selection, and scientific image inspection within a guided experience. Suggested destinations, collectible tools, and a weekly M101 challenge encourage continued learning.

The intended impact is to make authentic astronomical data approachable for students, educators, and curious beginners. Our team considered usability, accessibility, scientific accuracy, image resolution, bandwidth, and archive availability. Caching, bounded requests, and retry controls improve resilience, while explanations distinguish visual differences caused by wavelength or contrast from confirmed astronomical changes.
